passage: On Sunday evening in the kasba, Jeevan spread his notebook on the kitchen table in front of Papa. Harish read the dates, the times and the messages from the class group, the names, the laughing at Jeevan's torn bag. He read slowly. "You did well to keep this," Harish said. "None of it is your fault." Jeevan's shoulders eased. On Monday morning Papa walked into school with him. The class teacher went through the pages, thanked him, and took them to the counsellor before lunch. By afternoon the headmaster had called a meeting under the school's anti-bullying policy, the parents of the boys involved were sent for, and a teacher would sit in the class for the next weeks. Jeevan was no longer alone with it.

qa.q: Whom did Jeevan show the notebook to on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Jeevan showed the notebook to Papa, Harish, at the kitchen table.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after Papa said none of it was his fault?
qa.a: Jeevan felt relieved, as his shoulders eased, no longer carrying the blame or the secret.

qa.q: What else could Jeevan do if the messages continued after the meeting, and why?
qa.a: Jeevan could tell the class teacher or counsellor again the same day and keep adding to the record, because the policy gives the school a way to act again.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see the notebook?
qa.a: The class teacher sees clear, dated evidence that can be acted on, and is grateful Jeevan brought it, which is why it went to the counsellor before lunch.

grounding: The student shows the record to a parent and the class teacher, who involve the school counsellor and follow the anti-bullying policy, so the target does not carry the problem alone.

passage:
Emil had kept the list on his phone for three weeks: every time two boys in his class in Malmö pushed him at the lockers, hid his gym bag or called him names in the group chat. On Thursday evening he finally showed it to his mother, Olga, at the kitchen table.

She read it slowly, scrolling. Her face tightened, but her voice stayed calm. "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault."

The next morning she went with him to see his class teacher, Mr. Lindqvist, before first lesson. He read the list too, then asked Emil a few quiet questions. "I'm bringing in the school counsellor today," he said. "We have a plan for exactly this."

By Friday afternoon, the counsellor had met Emil, the boys' parents had been called, and the teacher had moved Emil's locker.

Emil slept better that night than he had in weeks.

qa.q: Who did Olga go with Emil to see before first lesson?
qa.a: She went with him to see his class teacher, Mr. Lindqvist.

qa.q: How might Emil have felt when he finally showed the list to his mother?
qa.a: He was probably nervous and scared of her reaction, and then relieved when she stayed calm and said it was not his fault.

qa.q: What else could the school do to follow up on this?
qa.a: The school could check in with Emil every week for a while, so any new incidents are caught quickly rather than left to him to report.

qa.q: How did Olga experience reading the list?
qa.a: Olga seemed upset, her face tightening, but she kept her voice calm so Emil would feel safe and supported.

grounding: Shows a student showing a record of bullying to a parent and the class teacher, who bring in the counsellor and follow the school's plan so the student is not alone.

passage:
The counsellor's room at Ujjwal's school in Lucknow had a box of tissues and a poster about kindness that everyone mocked. On Tuesday, Ujjwal sat there with his father, holding a notebook.

Inside were two months of dates: when seniors took his lunch, when they tripped him on the stairs, the messages in the class chat. Francis, his classmate, had helped him write it all down and had come along to the class teacher's desk that morning.

The class teacher, Mrs. Verma, read three pages and stopped. "Thank you for bringing this. You shouldn't have had to deal with it alone." She walked them to the counsellor herself.

The counsellor explained the school's anti-bullying steps: meetings with the seniors and their parents, staff watching the stairwell at break, and a weekly check-in with Ujjwal.

On the way out, Ujjwal's father put an arm around him. Francis walked a step behind, quietly smiling.

qa.a: Two months of dates: when seniors took his lunch, tripped him on the stairs and sent messages in the class chat.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt as the class teacher read the notebook?
qa.a: He was probably anxious about being believed, and then relieved when Mrs. Verma thanked him and took him straight to the counsellor.

qa.q: What could the school add to the steps the counsellor listed?
qa.a: It could make sure Ujjwal knows exactly which staff member to go to at break if anything happens, so help is quick.

qa.q: What was the day like for Francis?
qa.a: Francis probably felt proud and relieved, having helped write the record and seen adults take it seriously.

grounding: Shows a student bringing a written record of bullying to a parent and teacher, who involve the counsellor and follow the school's anti-bullying steps.
